```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      warning = FALSE)
# igraph is only Suggested, so every chunk that needs it is gated on it and the
# vignette still builds where it is missing.
has_igraph <- requireNamespace("igraph", quietly = TRUE)
```

Which emoji are used together is a network question, and `emoji_pairs()`
returns exactly the edge list a network package wants. The trap is that the
edge list it returns by default is mostly noise, and a layout draws noise as
confidently as it draws structure. This article builds an emoji network that
is worth drawing: weighted by an association measure, thresholded on
frequency, and checked against what the emoji-network literature says such
networks look like.

```{r setup}
library(tidyEmoji)
library(dplyr)

# the example corpus: 1,485 OASST2 messages, about half carrying emoji
posts <- oasst_messages
```

## Counts first, and why they are not enough

One row per pair of distinct emoji that appear in the same message, with the
number of messages in which they do:

```{r}
edges <- posts %>% emoji_pairs(text)
edges

edges %>% count(n, name = "pairs")
```

`r sum(edges$n == 1)` of the `r nrow(edges)` edges
(`r round(100 * mean(edges$n == 1), 1)`%) are a single message. A graph drawn
from all of them is one message's worth of evidence per line, and the few
heavy
edges belong to the emoji that are common everywhere, which pair with
everything because they are common, not because they are related.

## Weight by association, then threshold on frequency

Two changes fix this, and they do different jobs.

* **An association measure** scores each pair against what its two emoji's
  own frequencies predict, so a common emoji no longer wins every edge.
  `measure = "dice"` is `2 * n / (n1 + n2)`, with `n1` and `n2` the messages
  holding each emoji: 1 for a pair never seen apart, near 0 for a pair that
  is mostly apart. `"ppmi"` and `"log_odds"` are the alternatives; see
  `?emoji_pairs`.
* **A frequency threshold** removes the edges seen too rarely to mean
  anything. An association measure cannot do this on its own: a pair seen in
  one message, whose two emoji appear nowhere else, scores the maximum Dice
  of 1.

```{r}
weighted <- posts %>%
  emoji_pairs(text, measure = "dice") %>%
  filter(n >= 2)

weighted
```

That is the honest network for this corpus: `r nrow(weighted)` edges, where
the raw edge list had `r nrow(edges)`. Most of those came from a handful of
replies that tabulate dozens of emoji at once, which pair every emoji in the
table with every other; 1,485 messages holding 1,450 emoji are too few for a
network of more than a modest number of emoji, and it is better to know that
than to draw the whole edge list. A corpus of hundreds of thousands of
messages, or one pooled by user or by conversation with `doc_id`, gives a
graph with real structure.

## Into a network package

The edge list feeds `igraph` (or `tidygraph`) directly, with the association
measure as the edge weight:

```{r, eval = has_igraph}
g <- igraph::graph_from_data_frame(
  weighted[, c("item1", "item2", "dice", "n")], directed = FALSE)

igraph::vcount(g)
igraph::ecount(g)
igraph::components(g)$no
```

Community detection then groups emoji that are used together more than
chance; Louvain with the Dice weight is a reasonable default:

```{r, eval = has_igraph}
set.seed(2026)   # Louvain breaks ties at random; fix them for a stable answer
communities <- igraph::cluster_louvain(g, weights = igraph::E(g)$dice)
split(igraph::V(g)$name, igraph::membership(communities))
```

Drawing it is a job for a graph-plotting package. With `ggraph` installed, and
`ragg` as the graphics device so the glyphs render in colour:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(ggraph)
ggraph(g, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = dice), alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name), size = 6) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.3, 2)) +
  theme_void()
```

## Sanity checks for a bigger corpus

Studies of emoji co-occurrence networks on large Twitter samples (Fede et
al., 2018; Alsaif et al., 2021) report two properties, and both make good
checks that a network is measuring structure rather than sampling noise:

* the **degree distribution is heavy-tailed**: a few emoji connect to very
  many, most connect to a few;
* most emoji fall into **a handful of communities**.

Both are one line once the graph exists. On a network of a dozen nodes they
say little; on a real one, a degree table with no tail or a community count
close to the node count is a sign that the threshold was set too low:

```{r, eval = has_igraph}
table(igraph::degree(g))
length(communities)
```

## Directed sequences

`emoji_pairs(directed = TRUE)` orders each pair by first appearance in the
message, so the edge from one emoji to another counts the messages where the
first came first. The same measures apply to that ordered event, and
`emoji_ngrams()` gives the strictly consecutive version for Markov-style
models of emoji sequences.

## References

Alsaif H, Roesch P, Othman S (2021). Analyzing Co-occurrence Networks of
Emojis on Twitter. In *Intelligent Computing*, Springer.
<https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-80126-7_7>

Fede H, Herrera I, Mahdi Seyednezhad SM, Menezes R (2018). Representing Emoji
Usage Using Directed Networks: A Twitter Case Study. In *Complex Networks &
Their Applications VI*. <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-72150-7_67>
